projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div0.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of a cassette (copy) taped interview with Joe Zuckerman, conducted by Hal Phillips on ___________ ___, _____, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview took place in _____________________, Virginia, and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed by Marjorie Ziegler, RPR, CSR11382.

The reader should bear in mind that he or she is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of place, names, foreign words, and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Oral history interview of World War II veterans conducted by Harold Phillips for the Handley library archives and the Winchester Frederick County Historical society. Today is the 17th of July ________, and the veteran is Mr. Joe Zuckerman.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I was born in 1918. September the 9th. My father had come over from Russia when he was 16. He knew nothing about the American language. And he... parish was Waynesboro, Pennsylvania. Back then he called it being in the junk business. And he started with a push cart. Then we came to Hagerstown into Martinsberg and eventually into Winchester in 1917 with a horse and wagon, picking up junk. And I was born in 1918. And that's where we started. And we just had a little hole in the wall. And on Saturdays, I would go up to a little place on Baker Street. And all of us, of course, we were not very rich; and we didn't have much money. And sometimes, on Saturday, if we had enough money, I'd get a quarter. I went to John Kerr school and then to Handley.
And in my senior year, I loved sports. And in my senior year, I had to quit because of my father's health. And my brother, Sam, in his junior year also had to quit.

And we didn't have anything. We just started from scratch and did the best thing we could do. And then in , I wanted to be loyal. Well, I joined the National Guards. And I'll give you the reason I joined the National Guards was to go with a group of other fellows because we were going to Virginia Beach for maneuvers, and that was our vacation every two years. We were able to wear civilian clothes. Of course, the girls didn't particularly care for soldiers. So then after that, after we're getting close to 1940, that's when I had my hernia operation. Back then, they kept us in bed for weeks. And by the time I got out, the 29th Headquarters Division had moved out to maneuvers. So I wrote to Captain Hollis (ph) to see if I could get back in, and he said, "No." They were filled up. I said, "Well, I may as well go ahead and volunteer for a year." And there was a song, "Goodbye, Dear, I'll be Back in a Year."

Then I thought about suing the government because it was four and a half years later before I got out. So I went down to Camp Lee with a group from Winchester. And I was watching some of the troops, because I had National Guard training. And I walked into the -- my barracks one day.
And up on the wall was my name and a sign, Camp Edwards,
Massachusetts. Medic. So I went in to see the captain; and I said, "Captain, I think maybe you made a mistake.

I don't know anything about Medic." He said, "Well, I am sure there is a mistake." The next day, off I went to Camp Edwards, Massachusetts, in the Medics. And we stayed there. And then, again, I could wear civilian clothes. And I'd gone into Rockford, Illinois, which was about 30 miles from Camp Edwards.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you have any kind of boot training? Basic training --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yeah. We had some basic training. Medic training.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: When did you get that?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: While I was at --

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Fort Lee?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I did some. Then when I got to the camp and -- it wasn't Camp Edwards, it was Camp -- it was Illinois. Camp --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: That's Illinois.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: That's where I was. Camp Grant.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Camp Grant, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And we had our basic training there. Medic training.

Field hospital. And then I went in on the weekends. And Sunday morning, when I got up, I heard all this commotion outside: All soldiers report to camp immediately. And I said, "What in the hell is going on?" And the guy at the desk says...it was that day --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: December the 7th. Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Pearl Harbor had been bombed. And I said, "Where is Pearl Harbor?" We knew nothing about it. He says, "Get back to camp." I went back to camp. And, of course, we had been bombed. And then from there...

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Then you went to Fort Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And I went to Fort Leavenworth for about a week. And I didn't know were we were going, but we stayed there for a week.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And then I went to Camp Crowder, Missouri. We got there in December, just before Christmas. We were with the signal corps camp, and I was stationed at the hospital. And it was muddy and cold. And we were the first troops there. We got off and we went into the hospital. And I got a three-day pass with me and my buddies. And we went in to...

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: We went -- my memory is horrible.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Yeah, I know. His memory is not that good these days.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No. We went into Joplin. And we went into a bar.

And we were solo, and we were sitting there. And we had a couple of drinks. And I went to pay for it, and the bartender says, "See that couple over there?" And I says, "Yes." "They paid for the drinks, and they want to see you." So he went over and introduced himself. And he said, "Are you all going anywhere for Christmas?" And I said, "No. We just got here." They took us home. Had dinner for us. Spent the night, which I'll never forget, and then we went back to camp. And one of our duties -- of course, I was a private. Remember when I say we were one of the first troops there and we had coal furnaces, and we were supposed to each take a turn on firing the furnaces. Well, I don't know what happened, but I didn't get up in time. So the first thing I know is captain shaking me on the shoulder: "Zuckerman, you let the fire go out, and you burst the pipes." I thought oh, Jesus, now what. So what did they do, they made me fire the furnace every day. Every day. And finally, they were putting in a dental clinic over on the other part of the camp where a dental clinic would be, and I had to go about almost a mile to fire it every day. So one day, when I was over there, I saw this captain sitting there on the porch, reading. And I could tell he was just getting started. And I told him a story. I told him what had happened. I said, "Is there any chance that I could get out of this?" I said, "Jeez, I'm about done in." He said, "Well, let me see what I could do for you, Zuckerman." So he transferred me to a dental clinic which, again, I knew nothing about. And I started from scratch. I worked an opportunity. Surgery. And then those other troops started coming in. Then finally, they put me in charge of 90 men and told me that's what it's gonna be and made me the staff sergeant. And I stayed there for quite a while. Too long. And I don't know what had happened exceptin' the captain had been pals with me. He became major. And I remember we had a little Jewish boy that ________ __________. And they were all coming all the time. I was training them. And his feet were so bad that he should have never been able to get into the service. So we sent him off into the Army. Then I found out he got killed. So I went in to see Major Toul (ph), and I told him. I said, "Major, I don't know why you got me to stay here this long, but I've got to leave." So he said, "Okay." And then I went to Camp ___________, Illinois, a field hospital, took my training. And we were going to the Pacific. In the meantime, August the 1st of 1944, my mother passed away and I went home. And my father was in horrible shape.

And of course, all five of us were in the service, and we didn't have anything. And I went back to camp, and my attitude was not the best. And I was trying to find my clothes, and I got into an argument with the sergeant.

And I said, "We're getting ready to move out, and I don't have any clothes. I don't know where anything is." And just about that time, the 1st Sergeant came up to me and he said to me, "Sergeant, it looks like you're having a problem." And I told him what had happened. I said, "I lost my mother in July." He said, "Let's go over to the PX and have couple of beers." And his name was Bob Stoner (ph). So we did. And we sat there and talked and had a couple of drinks. And he said, "How would you like to join a hospital train?" Which I had never really heard of. He said, "I'm looking for a staff sergeant."

I says, "That's fine with me." So instead of going to the Pacific, instead of going to Normandy Beach -- all of this would have happened. I don't know how to explain it. So the first thing I know, I went to Camp Edwards, Massachusetts. And we had training there for hospital train. There were two nurses. Two medical officers.
The major was in charge or the lieutenant was in charge of the medical unit. And we left there just before Christmas.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Of what year, '44?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: '44. And we landed in Swansea, Wales, which by the way, we were bombed. And of course we were being bombed all the time we were going across. And I got sick as hell. I don't think I've ever been so sick.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Was it a big convoy at that port?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No. No. There was -- oh, there were some around; but we never really saw any. But of course, everything was blacked out. And landed in Swansea, Wales. Then we went to Scotland, to the barracks. There was two barracks.

We had about four or five coal stoves. And we stayed there awhile. And the Scottish people were really something else. Didn't have anything. No drinks. And I met this couple in Glasgow...girls. And another friend. >Myself. So when we went in, I would take my gas mask bag and fill it up with goodies, because we only got one coal shuttle a week in the department, and I'd come there with butter and candy. And we always give them some liquor.
And they couldn't get over it. And we went to a place called Green's Playhouse. And they played American music. It was all American music. It was beautiful.
And I was there. I loved to dance. And I was dancing with her. And all at once, I was bumping into everybody.
And I says to her these people don't know how to dance here. So finally, she said to me, Joe -- I told her she was hard to understand. I thought it was her language.

She said it was mine. And she said, "Joe, when we're here, we dance kind of clockwise." And a weekend later, we was supposed to go on down to the moors, two couples for a weekend; but when I got back to camp, I found out we were moving out. We were supposed to meet at Green's Playhouse. I had no way of telling her that we were leaving. And then when I got to Paris, I wrote and told her what had happened. And when we got there, in the middle of the hospital train, the whole group was just beginning to leave. And again, I knew nothing about a hospital train.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: How did you get from Scotland to Paris? What was that trip like?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I went to England and then we went across the channel.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: On a troop ship?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yeah, to France.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: The whole unit?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yeah, to France -- and children -- and then we got on a train to Paris. And we were still doing some training.

And I didn't -- and again I knew nothing about what was going to happen except I remember the troops that were leaving. They were saying you're really in for it. And while I was there, we got all our stuff together. And we were following Patton's army.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Battle of the Bulge. And we went to the front. And I got into Belgium.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Liege.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Liege, Belgium. And that was right on the French German border off of Germany and _______________. The first time we got there, they were bringing the wounded in in ambulances. And we were putting them on the train -- and the trains, which they were French -- and it was cold and there was condensation. And I'd never seen that. Legs off and arms off. I want to tell you, everybody got sick. Even though we weren't supposed to handle the wounded -- we were supposed to be in charge -- but we all did. But we didn't have much medical care. Had morphine. And ________________ and nurses were great. And we took them back to Paris. And the ones that were really in bad shape they put on the plane and sent to America. The wounded that were not so bad were put in hospitals in Paris. Then we'd of course get everything together again and then we'd head back up to the front.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: About how many would you have on a train?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Maybe a hundred. And it was an experience that I'll never forget. Again, I knew the world had gone wrong.
But I had luckily with all the things that happened to me, I didn't have to experience what a lot of them did.
I really, as I am sure you know, never even met __________________________________.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Well, I grew up with that. I was in the National Guards. So we did that until...then my brother was in Germany. And we corresponded and I wrote to him a couple of times and I said, Sam, we just can't get any cigarettes or candy here in Paris and would you mind sending me some. And he sent me a package. And then he got a three-day pass from his lieutenant who came up, and I introduced him to everybody on the train. And then I put my gas mask on. And I said I'm going to show you around a little. And Sam says to me, "God damn. What kind of a soldier are you?" So I went up to my favorite haunt and walked in and introduced myself and my brother.

And we went in the back room, and I opened up my gas mask. And I had cigarettes and I had candy and I had butter and I had sugar which I traded for cognac. And I can't tell you what Sam said to me. I didn't get any more goods from him. So it was good to see him. And he finally went back. And we continued up to the front until -- then Sam came in because he had a three-day pass because he was going to Japan. ___________________
_____________. And we had a little place where we had breakfast. By that time I was off the hospital train.
And I remember feeling a sad, goodbye. And the next day, the war ended. They dropped the bomb. So Sam didn't have to go. He got home before I did. And so I got home.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Do you remember how many trips you made with the hospital train?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Oh, we made maybe 30 or 40 trips. And then after the wounded, we started bringing back some psychos. It was interesting to talk to them because you really didn't know were they really psychos or -- and I talked to some of them. And then we brought back prisoners of war,

German prisoners of war; and they were either 15 and 16 or 60 and 70. There was nothing we could do. What could we do? We'd been in a fight. Of course we were forced to. And then after I...that was the end of that.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you have any attempts by the German air force to strafe your train or bomb your train?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Not ours, but they did. Of course we had a red cross on top, and they did strike one. But we were lucky. We really never thought a lot about it. You know. We were or 24 years old, and you know that a war is going on.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: But you had a job to do.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And I had a job to do.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did any of the prisoners cause any trouble at all?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Not a bit. None of them caused a bit of trouble.
They brought them in and put them in camps. And then after that, I was...I had a chateau while I was waiting to go home...and I had a chateau that I was living in.
Sheets. Hot water.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: How did you come across that?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Well, they just put me in it. I don't know why. But I was provo sergeant. And there was a liquor...oh, it was large.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I mean it was large. And they had...it was...belonged to the French. Captured by the Germans. Recaptured by the Americans. And I was put in charge of repacking.
And I mean it was all beautiful. Cognac. And liqueurs.
And then we had the French that would help me pack.
Well, on the end of it -- they just had these flimsy boxes. Then we would be putting them in heavy boxes and on the ends of it, return to the U.S. of America, for medicinal purpose.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Good for headaches; right?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Yes. Good for headaches.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: So I was tired. Well, I'm gonna...so when I'd go in,

I'd wear my raincoat. And I'd stick a couple bottles of cognac in the jacket and a couple in my sleeves. And I knew a girl at the Red Cross hotel there. And we would take them in so we would have it for the holidays. It just seemed like we ran out. Then I'll put some in my room. I tore out the floorboards because I had to hide them because we had inspection. So I had some there.
And then finally my time came up and I came home and I landed in New York. And then I went to Camp New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Fort Dix, I guess.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Fort Dix.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Could have been.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Could be.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And then I went from there to --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: ______________ and then straight out of Washington.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Fort Meade.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Fort Meade.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Fort Meade.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And then Meade. So I got my discharge. When I got home --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: You said that.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: -- we did have all five of the brothers. In fact, while we were in the service, all of us sent money home to keep the family home. My sister and my other sister and my father and mother were living in just a hole in the wall. I don't know whether you remember where Baker Street is.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: __________ Main Street. Well, that's where we started.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you have any trouble transitioning to civilian life again?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No, not really. Not really. I just knew that...you know, you could...of course at that time, you could go to college.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you use the GI bill?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No. I couldn't because we didn't have any -- I had to be there to do business.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: You were the oldest.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I was the oldest. In fact then I was the oldest of the kids because we all had came home and did the work, so I didn't use it. Then again we started with scratch.

And finally we moved from Baker Street over to Cameron Street, just a little hole in the wall. And my office was a bus. There was no telephone in there. Then we'd go out, then we'd use the torch -- since the phone rang -- and lay the torch down, went in, and I'd just call. Telephone. And then we had an old couple that didn't have a place to stay. I said okay. So they stayed in the bus at night. They didn't have anything.

That's the least we could do for them. And then we moved over to Kent Street where the oil companies were. The cities made the oil companies move out of town because there was...the oil and gas were around. So we took over those buildings. And the property still belongs to the railroad. So I think they've torn all the buildings down. So we went over there. And another friend from Johnstown that was in the scrap business -- he came down, as I remember very often; and for some reason or another, he took a liking to me. And he came down and he had a little Fairtrain luggage bag and a Cadillac and he smoked cigars and he smelled like hell. So he came back a couple more times. We lived in an apartment on Fairmont Avenue, $45 a month. _________________. And __________

_______ ______, I don't know whether you remember him or not. He was in the insurance business, and he lived next door. And he says to me -- he had a coal furnace. He said, "Joe, can you take care of my furnace?" I says, "Hell, no. I'm paying $45 a month." He says, "Well, you pay for the heat." One day -- he came down one day; and he said, Joe, you need a piece of equipment which is a bale to bale scrap iron laid on wire. And I told Dave, I says, "We don't have any money." He said, "I didn't ask you that." He said, "I'm going to buy you a TC-45 _______ baler." And he says, "You pay me back --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: -- a dollar a car. A ton a car." And we paid it off.
And then he came back a couple more times. And we stayed at the George Washington Hotel. And he said, "Joe, you need a house. [Interruption for recorder.] So he said,

You need a house." Again, I said, "Well, Dave, we don't have any money for a house." He said, "You look around and see what you can find; and when you find something you like, I'll come down and take a look at it." Well, I found a house on Middle Road. It was just being built.
And the previous owner lived there four years. $16,500.

So Dave said, "How much money do you need?" I says, "Well, I can get together...I'll need $10,000." He sent me a check for $10,000. He never signed a thing. He said, "Pay me back when you can." And out of that came the greatest relationship that I've ever had. Then when later on, we would drive up to Johnstown -- of course, we lived at 5__ Fremont Drive. We would go everywhere. He wouldn't let me drive. And I think it was at least _______________. He says, ___________ __________________________________ bracket?" I says, "No, not hardly." Then we'd go into a clothing store and he'd always want to buy me this and that and...

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Quite a friend.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you keep in contact with the man --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: -- that you served with while you were in the Army on the train and all that?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: You mentioned his name.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: He came here almost every year and we were just like brothers and his wife was just like a sister to Vicky.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Yes. __________ couple.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: We just had a great time together. Then they moved out of Staunton, but I don't know what happened with him.
But the Stolemans (ph) was just like part of our family.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And other than your brother, did you meet others from Winchester while you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: My brother Irvine.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Paul Irvine as well

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Hal Foreman (ph).

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Harold Foreman. I don't know whether you remember him or not. He was a......

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: I remember the name.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: He was a --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Worked at the post office, I think.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Post office. That was him. And then there was one other fella -- I can't remember -- that I met. But I know when we said good-bye, they're closer than your own family. I tell you there was a lot of tears shed when we said good-bye, because we didn't know what was going to happen. I mean, the war was over; and I knew we were going home. But on the hospital train, you were just like a family. Everybody shared. And we've never been any closer.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Joe, what decorations and awards did you receive?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: I didn't receive many awards, because again...I know I got a good conduct medal and then I think I got the European --

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Campaign Medal?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Campaign Medal, and another one.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: But anyway, I still got my dog tags.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Do you?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Still have them.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: The important thing.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: The important thing. But I was coming back from overseas -- I loved to play cards -- and I got into a crap game one day. We played day and night because we knew somebody was eating and somebody sleeping because we knew it was finished shift. And I got into a crap game one evening. And I says, "Well, I'm just going to see what I can do." And I just kept playing. And I kept --and my luck just continued. I won 1300-and-some-dollars and I stuffed it in my pocket and I quit. And a rookie, Charlie Pine (ph), from Pine Motor Company, because we were supposed to be one of the first to get -- get a car.
I mean, I don't know why I kept the check.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: I don't know either.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did that cover the cost of the car?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yeah. That was the cost of a car.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: There you go. Great. Okay. There's a mezuza.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Do you know what a mezuza is?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: No. What is that?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: A mezuza you put on the back of your front door, and it's good luck. It's the 10 Commandments.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: No. It's the blessing that upon the door post of that house and upon thy gate. It's a quotation from the Bible. It's on a little scroll.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Little kind of scroll

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And you carried that with you?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Well, it went on with the dog tag.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And this is the American theater. The European. Africa, and Mediterranean theater. One of them is the Victory Medal.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yes. I forgot about that --

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And these two I'm not familiar with; but you have the two clasps on this, so this must be the European theater.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: It still has the utensils that came with the mess kit.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: I guess. I guess. And I never think I saw the holes in the cigar box. Let me ____________________.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: We continued to grow. And we were on railroad property, and we needed more equipment; but the railroad wouldn't do anything at all. Then luckily, a piece of property came up for sale that belonged to Dr. Allen's wife, where we are now. I'm sure you've been to our place.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And we started with nothing. And since people had faith in us, we put in a baler. Shear. It was $184,000 just for the shear. Plus we bought two cranes. And we had to have all the work done by Shockey (ph). They put up the building for us. It was a hundred by three hundred. And the only thing I could see is people had faith, because we didn't have any -- we didn't have the money. And Bob Buckley (ph) ___________________ ________.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: I can't hear you.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Buckley __________ was right back where we are. And I told him, I says, Bob, we can't do anymore of the road work because we'd run out of money. And he said, "Joe, you can't let things go like that. There would be a mess by the time you get all of this stuff coming in." He says, "I'm going to finish the job for you. You pay me back when you can." I called _______________ __________.
And of course, he had the same problem. He says, "Oh, we're not going to let you down. You pay us when you can." And the same with Winchester Electric. But I never let 'em down.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes. Did they have faith you would pay it all?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Well, they did. You know, I always felt that. To tell the truth. That's the way I feel today. To lie to somebody is you're only kidding yourself.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes. Are all of the brothers still alive?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: No. My oldest brother, Irvine, died in 197__ of cancer of the prostate. And then my five brothers -- you're not supposed to tell neighbors. But he was the smartest of the five. Everything went wrong. His marriages went wrong. He landed in a far little town called _________ in Florida. Then after that, he got cancer. Then he finally came back and he stayed up here for a while, but he didn't have much time.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Would you mind telling us a little bit what he did during World War II?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Irving?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Irving.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: He was in the signal corps.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: That's the branch I was in. Signal corps.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yes. He was at Camp Crowder.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes. They had a signal base there.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Well, I'll have to tell you another little story then.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: When he came to Camp Crowder, well, of course I was really glad to see him. And we put pictures in the papers and all that. And I had a little place I used to go to on weekends. They had a swimming pool and cabins.

I says, "Irvine, I want to -- I'd like to take you along with me." He said, "Oh, no. I'm in basic training. I can't get away." I says, "Who is your 1st Sergeant?" So he gave me his name and I called him and I says this is Sergeant Zuckerman from the dental clinic. I says my brother is going _____ _______ ________ ___________. He says did you say dental clinic? I says, yeah. He says, man, you're the guy I'm looking for. I got a tooth that's giving me a fit. I says come in tomorrow. He went on the weekend. Just a little story that I had happen. And he didn't go overseas. And Charles didn't go overseas. Aaron (ph) was in the Navy, and he went in I think when we was about 16. Well, we were used to it.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: They had to sign for him to go in.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes. And a --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Sam didn't go overseas. He never ________ __________.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: But Aaron stayed in the United States?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Yes. And Charles did. He was in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Charleston?

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Charles.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female
sp.p: Charles.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: He stayed in.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Charles was the Air Force. Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Air Force. We had this business. Now we've been in business for 84 years. And I don't know whether you've been down to our plant lately or not......

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Not in the last few years. No.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Come down one day.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: We're not any longer a scrap pen. We are now a service organization. Because we started bringing all this steel in from overseas.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Oh, my, yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Some of it -- some of it, 30 steel mills, took Chapter ___________

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And......so then the President came up with the 2001 tariffs on incoming steel, and of course the country just raises hell.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: And now we charge. We charge for light goods.
Refrigerators. Stoves. And if the material is not right, we charge. And the whole thing was changed. And we just had a couple years that were really terrible.
And we had new equipment, but the prices had dropped.
The prices were really getting _________ ________

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Is there anything else you'd like to add about the --

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Well, in 1970s, the Patton (ph) Brothers owned -- they built the ___________ and the park. 217 acres. But they weren't getting along. One brother was doing all the back cutting, and the other one wasn't. So I finally saw an ad in the paper. Meadow-lake farm for sale. A hundred thousand dollars, 1970, which I didn't have enough money. And I tried to get somebody to help me and my brothers with some dough; and of course, it wouldn't work out. But anyway, I -- I bought it. And of course, I was a city boy. It completely changed my life.
Because I'm a conservation -- and people had given me hell over the 30 years, 32 years. I wanted to buy five acres and ten acres. But it was more than money to me.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joe Zuckerman
sp.p: Of course, I......people have just come up to me and loved it. And I don't know how many would say, if I owned this, Joe, I'd never leave.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yes. [Laughter.]
